intro.html: History, science and stories are full of order: what came first, what followed, what was coming next. This topic gathers the words that put things in time, and most of them are built from four Latin parts you can spot at a glance.

pre- and ante- = before (preliminary, predecessor, precursor, prescient, antecedent). post- = after (posterity, posthumous). sequ = follow (subsequent), and ced/cess = go (predecessor, successor, antecedent). The odd one out is harbinger, an old English word for someone sent ahead.

Two pairs are worth keeping straight: a predecessor held the job before you, and a successor holds it after you; something preliminary comes before the main event, and something subsequent comes after.

words.def: coming before the main part, to prepare for it
words.ex: The {preliminary} round of the spelling bee weeded out half the contestants.
words.ctx: Before building the full bridge, the engineers ran {preliminary} tests on a small model to see how it would handle strong wind.
words.etym: From Latin prae- (before) + limen (threshold): what comes before you step through the door.

mn.text: Before the big race, Dev stretches every limb, one by one: these are his {preliminary} exercises.

scene.alt: A runner in a headband stretches his arms before a race.

words.ex: The first storm knocked down a tree, and {subsequent} storms finished off the fence.
words.ctx: Her first cake sank in the middle, but {subsequent} attempts, made after she fixed the oven temperature, rose perfectly.
words.etym: From Latin subsequi, “to follow close after”: sub- (close to) + sequi (to follow).

mn.text: A sequel is the story that comes after the first one. Pip and Lila can’t wait for Part 2, due out the {subsequent} summer.

scene.alt: Two children cheer at a banner announcing Part 2 of a movie.

words.def: a person who held a job or role before someone else
words.ex: The new coach kept many of the drills from her {predecessor}.
words.ctx: Unlike his {predecessor}, who rarely left the office, the new principal visited every classroom during his first week.
words.etym: From Late Latin praedecessor: prae- (before) + decessor (one who has left an office), from decedere (to go away).

mn.cue: PRE-DESK-essor: at the DESK before you
mn.text: Edwin carries his box out the door, and Lin sits down at his old desk; the one who had the desk before her is her {predecessor}.

scene.alt: An old professor carries his box out of the office while a woman sits down at his old desk.

words.def: a person or thing that follows another in a role or place
words.ex: The old queen named her niece as her {successor}.
words.ctx: The retiring baker trained Jamal for a full year so that her {successor} would know every recipe by heart when he took over the shop.
words.etym: From Latin successor, from succedere (to come after): sub- (close after) + cedere (to go).

mn.text: In the relay, Dev hands the torch to Maya, who runs the next stretch: Maya is his {successor}.

scene.alt: A runner hands a torch to the next runner, who takes off.

words.def: something that comes before and leads to something else
words.ex: The old telegraph was an {antecedent} of today’s text message.
words.ctx: In the sentence “Maya lost her scarf,” the {antecedent} of the pronoun her is Maya, the word that comes before it and that it points back to.

roots.means: being or doing (a noun or adjective ending)

words.etym: From Latin antecedere, “to go before”: ante- (before) + cedere (to go).
words.note: In grammar, the antecedent is the word a pronoun stands for.

mn.cue: the ANT-ecedent: the ANT that goes BEFORE
mn.text: The first ant marches ahead, and all the others follow behind it; the one that goes before is the {antecedent}.

scene.alt: A line of ants marches along, led by the first ant.

words.def: something that came earlier and led the way to a later thing
words.ex: The abacus was a {precursor} of the calculator.
words.ctx: Long before the first airplane, the glider was its {precursor}, proving that a person could ride the air on fixed wings.
words.etym: From Latin praecursor, “forerunner”: prae- (before) + currere (to run).

mn.text: Long before cars, horse-drawn carts rumbled down the roads; the cart ran ahead of the car in history. It was a {precursor}.

scene.alt: A horse-drawn cart on one side and a car on the other, with an arrow from the cart to the car.

words.def: a sign or messenger of what is coming
words.ex: The first crocus poking through the snow is a {harbinger} of spring.
words.ctx: The sudden silence of the birds was a {harbinger} of the storm; within minutes, the sky turned dark and the rain began.
words.etym: From Middle English herbergere, a person sent ahead to find lodgings for travelers.

mn.cue: HARK! A sign of what’s coming
mn.text: “Hark! Spring is on its way!” says the first butterfly over the melting snow; it is a {harbinger} of spring.

scene.alt: A butterfly flutters over the melting snow where the first flowers are coming up.

words.def: knowing or sensing what will happen before it does
words.ex: Her {prescient} warning about the leaky roof saved our books from the rain.
words.ctx: Grandpa’s advice that everyone should learn to type seemed odd in 1975, but it proved {prescient}; within twenty years, nearly every office job required a keyboard.
words.etym: From Latin praescire, “to know beforehand”: prae- (before) + scire (to know).

mn.text: On a cloudless morning, Granny Mae packs an umbrella; by noon it pours, and she is the only one dry. She was {prescient}.

scene.alt: A grandmother stays dry under her umbrella while a teen beside her is caught in the sudden rain.

words.def: all the people of the future; later generations
words.ctx: The museum carefully preserves the old letters, not only for today’s visitors but for {posterity}, so that people a hundred years from now can read them too.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

words.etym: From Latin posteritas, from posterus (coming after), from post (after).

mn.cue: a POSTER for the FUTURE: POSTER-ity
mn.text: The class seals a poster in a time capsule for the children of a hundred years from now: they are saving it for {posterity}.

scene.alt: Two children bury a time capsule holding a poster addressed to the future.

words.def: happening or given after a person’s death
words.ex: The poet’s best-known book was a {posthumous} collection, printed after she died.
words.ctx: The painter sold only one picture in her lifetime; her fame was {posthumous}, growing only after her death, when museums began to collect her work.
words.etym: From Latin postumus, “last, born after the father’s death”; the h was added later by people who linked it with humus (earth).
words.note: Say POS-chuh-mus: the h is silent.

mn.cue: POST = after: praise that comes AFTER a life
mn.text: Great-Grandma Rose painted all her life, but her pictures won prizes only after she had passed away: her fame was {posthumous}.

scene.alt: A grandmother and a girl admire a prize-winning painting in a museum.

head: before
after
rows: antecedent, precursor (came first, led to it)
after.cap: Before and after, side by side.

after.html: prescient has nothing to do with present. It is pre- (before) + sci (know), the same sci as in science: a prescient person knows before. And posthumous is said POS-chuh-mus; the h is silent.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The new mayor praised her {predecessor} for leaving the town’s budget in good shape.

after.cap: The one who held the job before her is her predecessor.

items.q: Ms. Lin was the librarian until 2020; then Mr. Felix took over. Ms. Lin is Mr. Felix’s…
items.why: She held the job before him, so she is his predecessor, and he is her successor.

items.q: Using the same story, Mr. Felix is Ms. Lin’s…
items.why: He followed her in the job, so he is her successor.

items.q: True or false: in posthumous, the h is pronounced.
items.why: False. Say POS-chuh-mus. The h crept into the spelling long ago, but it is silent.
Sci means know, as in science and conscious. Prescient means knowing before something happens.
